title: Fix doc building to use astropy source
description:
Fixing this was more subtle than I realized, but this PR now finally makes the sphinx build operate consistently.  Now, `python setup.py build_sphinx` always uses the version of astropy in the build directory, while `make html` in the `docs` directory will use the installed version.

As part of this, a critical bug is fixed that in the past meant you _had_ to have the C extensions installed via `python setup.py develop` or `python setup.py build_ext --inplace` to get the docs to build.  That is no longer the case.

This closes #134 .

expected_findings.description: Reviewer `mdboom` reported that the documentation build output was placed in an incorrect nested directory (`docs/docs/_build/html`). Reviewer `embray` confirmed seeing the same behavior. The author (`eteq`) later acknowledged the issue, identified the cause as changing the directory within the subprocess (`os.chdir('docs')`) without properly handling relative paths, and provided a fix.

title: Should missing .c files from .pyx raise an error?
description:
I came across something surprising when setting up a new machine which didn't yet have Cython on it.

If a `.c` file generated from a `.pyx` file is missing and Cython is not available, it merely logs a warning.  Shouldn't this be an exception, since it means we can't build a working astropy?  (It still works to build astropy from a source tarball -- those users still don't need to have Cython installed -- this is only a problem with a `git` checkout.)

```
                        log.warn('Could not find c file {0} for {1}; skipping '
                                 'extension {2}.'.format(cfn, pyxfn, ext.name))
```

-                        log.warn('Could not find c file {0} for {1}; skipping '
-                                 'extension {2}.'.format(cfn, pyxfn, ext.name))
-                        del extensions[idx]
-                        break
+                        raise IOError(
+                            'Could not find C file {0} for Cython file {1}; '

expected_findings.description: Reviewer 'astrofrog' pointed out that the `format` string in the `IOError` message only had two placeholders (`{0}`, `{1}`) but was being passed three arguments (`cfn`, `pyxfn`, `ext.name`). In a subsequent comment, 'astrofrog' suggested how to correct the message to include the third argument. The author 'mdboom' acknowledged this as a "Good catch" and confirmed they fixed the message.

CRVAL4  =   1.000000000000E+00
CDELT4  =   1.000000000000E+00
CRPIX4  =   1.000000000000E+00
CUNIT4  = '        '

```

with:

```
In [1]: from astropy.io import fits

In [2]: header = fits.Header.fromtextfile('header.hdr')

In [3]: from astropy import wcs

In [4]: w = wcs.WCS(header)
```

the `naxis` attribute has the wrong value:

```
In [5]: print w.naxis
4
```

as I would imagine `NAXIS` takes precedence over anything else. If I try and access `naxis3` for example, I have issues:

```
In [6]: print w.naxis3

----> 1 print w.naxis3

AttributeError: 'WCS' object has no attribute 'naxis3'
```

as expected.

title: Separate color printing from coloring text
description: This is the implementation of #413 -- I've just separated the code that wraps strings with the ANSI color codes from the code that actually prints to the terminal. @mdboom mentioned that this was an implementation choice (see #101) but I think it's fine to have a separate "private" method to do this.

+    """
+    Returns a string wrapped in ANSI color codes for coloring the
+    text in a terminal::
+    
+        colored_text = color_text('Here is a message', 'blue')
+    
+    This won't actually effect the text until it is printed to the
+    terminal.
+    
+    Parameters
+    ----------
+    text : str
+        The string to return, bounded by the color codes.
+    color : str
+        An ANSI terminal color name. Must be one of:
+        black, red, green, brown, blue, magenta, cyan, lightgrey,
+        default, darkgrey, lightred, lightgreen, yellow, lightblue,
+        lightmagenta, lightcyan, white, or '' (the empty string).
+    """
+    color_mapping = {
+        'black': '0;30',

+        'green': '0;32',
+        'brown': '0;33',
+        'blue': '0;34',
+        'magenta': '0;35',
+        'cyan': '0;36',

+        'lightblue': '1;34',
+        'lightmagenta': '1;35',
+        'lightcyan': '1;36',
+        'white': '1;37'}
+    
+    color_code = color_mapping.get(color, '0;39')
+    return u'\033[{0}m{1}\033[0m'.format(color_code, text)
+

     Prints colors and styles to the terminal uses ANSI escape

title: Add sections Getting help and Reporting issues to main doc index
description:
This adds information on getting help and reporting issues, expanding somewhat on the text from www.astropy.org. 

I think it's good to have this info on the landing page for astropy docs.  The Getting Started section is another candidate location that would make sense if people don't think this belongs on the main index.

Preview at http://hea-www.harvard.edu/~aldcroft/tmp/astropy/html/index.html

    development/scripts
    development/sphinxext
 
+***********************
+Getting help
+***********************
+
+If you want to get help or discuss issues with other Astropy users, you can
+sign up for the `astropy <http://mail.scipy.org/mailman/listinfo/astropy>`_
+mailing list.  Alternatively, the `astropy-dev
+<http://groups.google.com/group/astropy-dev>`_ list is where you should go to
+discuss more technical aspects of Astropy with the developers.
+
+***********************
+Reporting issues
+***********************
+
+If you have come across something that you believe is a bug, please open a
+ticket in the Astropy `issue tracker
+<http://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues>`_, and we will look into it
+promptly.
+
+Please try to include an example that demonstrates the issue and will allow the
+developers to reproduce and fix the problem.  If you are seeing a crash

expected_findings.description: Reviewer `astrofrog` suggested moving the newly added sections (introduced at the bottom of the page in commit 63b57a0) higher up, specifically suggesting placing them before the developer documentation or in the 'Getting started' section. Reviewer `embray` agreed. The author (`taldcroft`) discussed the options and acknowledged the suggestion by implementing the move in a subsequent commit.

Reviewer `eteq` identified a Sphinx build warning caused by the specific reStructuredText link format `` `astropy <...>`_ `` introduced in the first commit. The reviewer explained the likely cause (conflict with the package name) and suggested a specific textual change to the link format to resolve the warning. The author implemented this exact suggestion in a subsequent commit.

expected_findings.description: Reviewer `eteq` pointed out that while `spectral_density` could handle energy units (`keV`) in its *argument*, it failed when trying to convert *to* a unit with an energy denominator (`erg/s/cm^2/keV`). This highlighted a missing piece of functionality required for X-ray astronomy units. Reviewer `pllim` later confirmed (2014-04-07T18:24:25) that this unit combination was indeed undefined within the existing `spectral_density` implementation and suggested expanding it.

Reviewer `eteq` questioned whether the `spectral_density` equivalency should work for units beyond the explicitly defined flux/luminosity densities (e.g., for integrated energy per spectral bin). This pointed out a limitation in the implementation's generality, suggesting it could be broadened to handle any compatible numerator unit while converting the spectral denominator (e.g., `/Hz` to `/AA`). The discussion confirmed this generalization was desirable but not implemented.

expected_findings.description: The reviewer (`embray`) pointed out that using `is False` and `is True` for NumPy boolean arrays (introduced as a PEP8 fix in the PR) is incorrect because NumPy uses its own boolean types (`np.False_`, `np.True_`) which are not identical to Python's built-in `False` and `True`. This would lead to incorrect test logic and failures. The author (`astrofrog`) acknowledged this and proposed using `np.all(~self.a.mask)` and `np.all(self.b.mask)` as a correct and PEP8-compliant alternative, which was subsequently implemented.

The reviewer (`embray`) suggested removing the explicit `+` operator used for string concatenation within the `ImportError` message, noting that implicit concatenation works within parentheses and is cleaner. The author (`astrofrog`) acknowledged this suggestion ("Done") and implemented the change.

title: Added inverse to some models and SCompositeModel.
description:
This PR adds `inverse()` method to some models.
The idea is to add analytical inverse to models when possible as `Model.inverse()` and change the flag `Model.has_inverse` to `True`.
This is different from `Model.invert()` which will implement a general iterative method to calculate the inverse of some input.
The `inverse` method returns an object which performs the inverse transformation.

The `SCompositeModel` which combines models in series then has an inverse if all children models have inverse.
Is this acceptable?

title: Column with no name cannot be printed
description:
@taldcroft - Currently, printing a `Column` with its name not set gives a `TypeError`:

```
from astropy.table import Column
print(Column([1.,2.]))
ERROR: TypeError: object of type 'NoneType' has no len() [astropy.table.pprint] 
```

This can be fixed quite easily in `pprint.py`, in `_pformat_col_iter`, by setting the heading for the column to `''` or a space or so when `name is None`. But before I do so, I thought I would first check that this would be the idea.

The reviewer (`taldcroft`) suggested alternative, more robust ways (`.startswith` or `in`) to assert the content of the exception message in the tests, rather than relying on character counting via slicing (`[0:40]`). title: Fix --open-files test with Python 3.3 and newer
description:
Currently, the pytest plugin for open files uses a function that has been deprecated since [this commit](https://hg.python.org/cpython/rev/b81ddaf0db47) in Python 3.3.

Specifically, running `python setup.py test --open-files` gives: (shortening the long lines)

```
astropy/tests/pytest_plugins.py:431: 
 _

    def _get_open_file_list():
        fsencoding = sys.getfilesystemencoding()

        sproc = subprocess.Popen(
            ['lsof -F0 -n -p {0}'.format(os.getpid())],
            shell=True, stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
        output = sproc.communicate()[0].strip()
        files = []
        for line in output.split(b'\n'):
            columns = line.split(b'\0')
            mapping = {}
            for column in columns:
                if len(column) >= 2:
                    mapping[column[0:1]] = column[1:]

            if (mapping.get(b'f') and
                mapping.get(b'a', b' ') != b' ' and
                    mapping.get(b't') == b'REG'):
                # Ignore extension modules -- they may be imported by a
                # test but are never again closed by the runtime.  That's
                # ok.
>               for suffix, mode, filetype in imp.get_suffixes():
                    if mapping[b'n'].decode(fsencoding).endswith(suffix):

astropy/tests/pytest_plugins.py:418: 
 _

    def get_suffixes():
        warnings.warn('imp.get_suffixes() is deprecated; use the constants '
                      'defined on importlib.machinery instead',
>                     DeprecationWarning, 2)
E       DeprecationWarning: imp.get_suffixes() is deprecated; use the constants defined on importlib.machinery instead

/usr/lib64/python3.3/imp.py:58: DeprecationWarning
= 96 skipped, 11 xfailed, 5561 error in 200.14 seconds =
```

While `python2.7 setup.py test --open-files` only results in:

```
= 1 failed, 8090 passed, 149 skipped, 43 xfailed, 3 xpassed in 478.00 seconds =
```

(the one failure looks like a numerical issue in `TestFittable1DModels.test_deriv_1D`)

After this PR, the numbers for python 3 go down to:

```
= 1 failed, 5482 passed, 140 skipped, 42 xfailed, 3 xpassed in 292.71 seconds =
```

and is unchanged for python2.

To prevent this from happening again, I also enabled Travis to check for opened files with the newest python2 and python3 versions.

description:

It gives the impression that everyone should be catching `AstropyUserWarning` for any warnings, but I think that's incorrect: that's only when it's actually a _user_ issueing the warning that that should be used, right?  `AstropyWarning` is what astropy actually throws in real code.

+Astropy includes its own warning classes,

+on which all warnings from Astropy are based.  So one can also ignore warnings
+from Astropy (while still allowing through warnings from other libraries

 Astropy also issues warnings when deprecated API features are used.  If you

expected_findings.description: The reviewer (`embray`) pointed out that the initial documentation change, while technically correct about using `AstropyWarning` to catch all warnings, lacked necessary clarification about the intended distinction between `AstropyWarning` and `AstropyUserWarning`. The PR author (`eteq`) later acknowledged this and pushed a commit specifically addressing these suggested clarifications, which the reviewer then approved.

title: Change simple_table to use 64-bit int and float instead of 32-bit
description:
The table helper function `simple_table()` was returning a table with 32-bit int and 32-bit float columns.  Now it returns 64-bit values which are more "normal" in everyday use.

Long version:
While there isn't anything specifically wrong with that, it turns out that `np.searchsorted` is quite slow for something like `np.searchsorted(np.arange(1e7, dtype=np.float32), 100.0)` because it casts the input array to the type of the search value (https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/5370).  I lost some time trying to figure out why table indexing and np.searchsorted were so slow when in fact it was just that numpy issue.  In order to prevent future digressions because 32-bit values are not the norm, I want to change `simple_table` (which I use all the time in quick testing and development).

expected_findings.description: The reviewer (mhvk) noted that the changes introduced in the initial commit caused multiple test failures. The author subsequently fixed these failures in a later commit (0ff24a9) and confirmed "Passing tests now", implicitly acknowledging and addressing the issue raised by the reviewer. The failures occurred because tests relied on the previous 32-bit output types of `simple_table`, and the change to 64-bit types broke this expectation (interface).

title: Add step to affiliated package release instructions
description:
This PR just adds a checking step to the release instructions for affiliated packages.  This was triggered by experiences from @bmorris3 doing a first release for astroplan, and issues I've encountered when doing astropy releases.

The step added tells the maintainer that before they do the final pypi register/upload, they should try to install into a completely fresh environment with dependency combinations users are likely to have. My main motivation for adding this is that it's not that uncommon for developer's "regular" environment to have all kinds of packages that may or may not be out-of-date or installed weirdly which mask problems that show up for a more typical user (who often has just the standard dependencies from conda or whatever).  I know I've caught subtle bugs this way before (and we did so again in the astroplan release), so I'm suggesting it here at least as an "optional" step.

cc @astrofrog @cdeil
diff:
diff --git a/docs/development/affiliated-packages.rst b/docs/development/affiliated-packages.rst
index 1c102a66079..07488cb78a2 100644
--- a/docs/development/affiliated-packages.rst
+++ b/docs/development/affiliated-packages.rst
@@ -501,8 +501,30 @@ replace ``CHANGES.rst`` by ``CHANGES.md`` in the instructions.
 
         git commit -m "Back to development: <next_version>"
 
-#. Check out the release commit with ``git checkout v<version>``. Run
-   ``git clean -fxd`` to remove any non-committed files, then either release with::
+#. Check out the release commit with ``git checkout v<version>``.
+   Run ``git clean -fxd`` to remove any non-committed files.
+
+#. (optional) Run the tests in a virtual environment that mocks up a
+   "typical user" scenario.  This is not strictly necessary because you ran the
+   tests above, but it can sometimes be useful to catch subtle bugs that might
+   come from you using a customized developer environment.  For more on setting
+   up virtual environments, see :ref:`virtual-envs`, but for the sake of example
+   we will assume you're using `Anaconda <http://conda.pydata.org/docs/>`_. Do::
+
+       conda create -n myaffilpkg_rel_test astropy <any more dependencies here>
+       source activate myaffilpkg_rel_test
+       python setup.py install
+       cd <anywhere not your package's source directory>
+       python -c 'import myaffilpkg; myaffilpkg.test()'
+       source deactivate
+       cd <back to your source>
+
+   You may want to repeat this for other combinations of dependencies if you think
+   your users might have other relevant packages installed.  Assuming the tests
+   all pass, you can proceed on.
+
+#. If you did the previous step, do ``git clean -fxd`` again to remove anything
+   you made there. Then either release with::
 
         python setup.py register build sdist --format=gztar upload

expected_findings.description: Reviewer `mdboom` pointed out that using "virtual environment" could be confusing as it might imply the specific `virtualenv` tool, whereas the example uses `conda`. The reviewer suggested using the more generic term "environment". The developer acknowledged this in the commit message of the fixing commit.

Reviewer `embray` suggested an alternative approach for the pre-release testing step. Instead of installing directly from the source directory (`python setup.py install`), the reviewer proposed building the source distribution (`sdist`) first and then installing and testing from the resulting tarball using `pip`. The developer later acknowledged this suggestion in a comment ("AFter thinking about it I liked @embray's sdist approach better, so I modified this to reflect that.") and implemented it.

I'd appreciate if @patti and/or @cdeil could take a look at this and double-check I didn't say anything wrong (or if you think may change made it _less_ clear I'm happy to here that and make changes appropriately!)

title: Add get_moon function to astropy.coordinates using the erfa.plan94
description: Trying to replicate the `get_sun` function to add the `get_moon` function using `erfa.plan94` to get the position and velocity of the Earth-Moon Barycenter.
diff:
diff --git a/astropy/constants/si.py b/astropy/constants/si.py
index 0aada8ff074..876c502ff14 100644
--- a/astropy/constants/si.py
+++ b/astropy/constants/si.py
@@ -156,3 +156,7 @@ M_earth = Constant('M_earth', "Earth mass", 5.9742e24, 'kg', 0.00005e24,
 R_earth = Constant('R_earth', "Earth equatorial radius", 6.378136e6, 'm',
                    0.0000005e6, "Allen's Astrophysical Quantities 4th Ed.",
                    system='si')
+
+# Moon mass
+M_moon = Constant('M_moon', "Moon mass", 7.353e22, 'kg', 0.0005e22,
+                 "Allen's Astrophysical Quantities 4th Ed.", system='si')
diff --git a/astropy/coordinates/funcs.py b/astropy/coordinates/funcs.py
index 308ec29eb18..21e701cfe12 100644
--- a/astropy/coordinates/funcs.py
+++ b/astropy/coordinates/funcs.py
@@ -21,9 +21,10 @@ from .sky_coordinate import SkyCoord
 from .builtin_frames import GCRS, PrecessedGeocentric
 from .representation import SphericalRepresentation, CartesianRepresentation
 from .builtin_frames.utils import get_jd12
+from .. import constants as const
 
 __all__ = ['cartesian_to_spherical', 'spherical_to_cartesian', 'get_sun',
-           'concatenate', 'get_constellation']
+           'get_moon', 'concatenate', 'get_constellation']
 
 
 def cartesian_to_spherical(x, y, z):
@@ -170,6 +171,61 @@ def get_sun(time):
     return SkyCoord(cartrep, frame=GCRS(obstime=time))
 
 
+def get_moon(time):
+    """
+    Determines the location of the moon at a given time (or times, if the input
+    is an array `~astropy.time.Time` object), in geocentric coordinates.
+
+    Parameters
+    ----------
+    time : `~astropy.time.Time`
+        The time(s) at which to compute the location of the moon.
+
+    Returns
+    -------
+    newsc : `~astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord`
+        The location of the moon as a `~astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord` in the
+        `~astropy.coordinates.GCRS` frame.
+
+
+    Notes
+    -----
+    The algorithm for determining the moon/earth distance is based on finding 
+    the heliocentric position of the earth and earth-moon barycentre using the
+    simplified version of VSOP2000 and the algorithm due to J. L. Simon et al.,
+    respectively, which are both part of ERFA.
+    """
+    earth_pv_helio, earth_pv_bary = erfa.epv00(*get_jd12(time, 'tdb'))
+    emb_pv = erfa.plan94(*get_jd12(time, 'tdb'), np=3)
+
+    # We have to manually do aberration because we're outputting directly into
+    # GCRS
+    earth_p = earth_pv_helio[..., 0, :]
+    earth_v = earth_pv_helio[..., 1, :]
+
+    emb_p = emb_pv[..., 0, :]
+    emb_v = emb_pv[..., 1, :]
+    moon_p = float((const.M_moon+const.M_earth)/const.M_moon)*emb_p - \
+             float(const.M_earth/const.M_moon*earth_p)
+    moon_v = float((const.M_moon+const.M_earth)/const.M_moon)*emb_v - \
+             float(const.M_earth/const.M_moon*earth_v)
+    dmoon = np.sqrt(np.sum((moon_p-earth_p)**2, axis=-1))
+    invlorentz = (1-np.sum((moon_v-earth_v)**2, axis=-1))**-0.5
+    properdir = erfa.ab((earth_p-moon_p)/dmoon.reshape(-1, 1),
+                        earth_v-moon_v,
+                        dmoon,
+                        invlorentz)
+
+    x = -dmoon*properdir[..., 0] * u.AU
+    y = -dmoon*properdir[..., 1] * u.AU
+    z = -dmoon*properdir[..., 2] * u.AU
+
+    if time.isscalar:
+        cartrep = CartesianRepresentation(x=x[0], y=y[0], z=z[0])
+    else:
+        cartrep = CartesianRepresentation(x=x, y=y, z=z)
+    return SkyCoord(cartrep, frame=GCRS(obstime=time))
+
 
 def concatenate(coords):
     """

expected_findings.description: The author initially noted significant inaccuracies (`sharadmirani`, 2016-03-28T12:00:28+00:00). Reviewers `mhvk` and `eteq` confirmed that the chosen approach (using `erfa.plan94` for the EMB and subtracting Earth's position) is fundamentally unsuitable for calculating the Moon's position accurately due to the magnification of errors and potential numerical issues ("machine-level errors in the subtraction"). They identified this as a significant flaw in the implementation for `get_moon` and suggested the approach was better suited for planets (`get_planet`). This confirmed the functional defect discovered by the reviewers.

title: Fix error message when accessing the component of a frame
description:
I recently noticed the following behavior that I found surprising:

```
>>> c_wdata = ICRS(1*u.deg, 2*u.deg)
>>> c_wdata.ra
<Longitude 1.0 deg>
>>> c_nodata = ICRS()
>>> c_nodata.data
ValueError: The frame object "<ICRS Frame>" does not have associated data
>>> c_nodata.ra
AttributeError: 'ICRS' object has no attribute '_rep_cache'
```

I think it's pretty clear that in this context asking `c.ra` is a request for data, and the more useful error message is "this frame has no data" rather than an opaque error about not finding the representation cache.

So this PR fixes that by being a bit more careful in the base frame's `__getattr__` about asking for a representation.  So after this PR, the above changes to:

```
>>> c_nodata.ra
ValueError: The frame object "<ICRS Frame>" does not have associated data
```

I think this is more "correcting some possible confusion" than a bug, so I haven't labeled it as a bug, nor added a changelog entry (as it strikes me as more like "documentation").  But @adrn, @astrofrog, or @taldcroft, feel free to say otherwise if you think it should get a changelog entry.
diff:
diff --git a/astropy/coordinates/baseframe.py b/astropy/coordinates/baseframe.py
index abe7e1989fc..9215558adf5 100644
--- a/astropy/coordinates/baseframe.py
+++ b/astropy/coordinates/baseframe.py
@@ -1037,9 +1037,18 @@ class BaseCoordinateFrame(object):
             raise AttributeError("'{0}' object has no attribute '{1}'"
                                  .format(self.__class__.__name__, attr))
 
-        rep = self.represent_as(self.representation, in_frame_units=True)
-        val = getattr(rep, self.representation_component_names[attr])
-        return val
+        if self._data is None:
+            if attr in self.representation_component_names.keys():
+                # this raises the "no data" error by design - doing it this way
+                # means we don't have to replicate the error message here
+                self.data
+            else:
+                raise AttributeError("'{0}' object has no attribute '{1}'"
+                                     .format(self.__class__.__name__, attr))
+        else:
+            rep = self.represent_as(self.representation, in_frame_units=True)
+            val = getattr(rep, self.representation_component_names[attr])
+            return val
 
     def __setattr__(self, attr, value):
         repr_attr_names = set()
diff --git a/astropy/coordinates/tests/test_frames.py b/astropy/coordinates/tests/test_frames.py
index dcf570b29de..283bd09751e 100644
--- a/astropy/coordinates/tests/test_frames.py
+++ b/astropy/coordinates/tests/test_frames.py
@@ -531,9 +531,11 @@ def test_nodata_error():
     from ..builtin_frames import ICRS
 
     i = ICRS()
-    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
+    with pytest.raises(ValueError) as excinfo:
         i.data
 
+    assert 'does not have associated data' in str(excinfo.value)
+
 def test_len0_data():
     from ..builtin_frames import ICRS
 
@@ -673,3 +675,24 @@ def test_getitem_representation():
     c = ICRS([1, 1] * u.deg, [2, 2] * u.deg)
     c.representation = 'cartesian'
     assert c[0].representation is representation.CartesianRepresentation
+
+
+def test_component_error_useful():
+    """
+    Check that a data-less frame gives useful error messages about not having
+    data when the attributes asked for are possible coordinate components
+    """
+    from ..builtin_frames import ICRS
+
+    i = ICRS()
+
+    with pytest.raises(ValueError) as excinfo:
+        i.ra
+    assert 'does not have associated data' in str(excinfo.value)
+
+    with pytest.raises(AttributeError) as excinfo1:
+        i.foobar
+    with pytest.raises(AttributeError) as excinfo2:
+        i.lon  # lon is *not* the component name despite being the underlying representation's name
+    assert "object has no attribute 'foobar'" in str(excinfo1.value)
+    assert "object has no attribute 'lon'" in str(excinfo2.value)

expected_findings.description: The reviewer (`taldcroft`) pointed out that the `else` block raising an `AttributeError` within the newly added `if self._data is None:` check seemed redundant, as a similar check and exception raise existed just before this new block (checking if `attr not in self.representation_component_names`). The author (`eteq`) acknowledged this ("Oh good catch", "silly mistake") and agreed to fix it.

title: Removing deprecated code from io.fits.header
description:
This is a rebased ad squashed version of #4445 that was milestoned as 1.2. 
I believe @embray gave the green light pending the changelog entry back in Jan, thus it would be nice to get this in the release.

Closes #4445, closes #4429 and most probably #2594, too.

title: Make footprint_to_file more useful
description:
I discovered `WCS.footprint_to_file` recently while looking for a similar method, but found a few issues that I attempt to fix here:

- The default coordinate system was 'linear', which was not working with aplpy/pyregion. Instead I changed to use by default the one from `wcs.radesys` (typically ICRS or FK5) and added a new parameter to allow to overwrite this coordinate system. See the [supported coordinate systems](http://ds9.si.edu/doc/ref/region.html#RegionFileFormat), is it useful to add a check that the value is correct ?

- When using the method multiple times, the new string were appended to the old ones,  with the global parameters written multiple times. So I changed to overwrite the file ('w' instead of 'a'). I thought about adding a parameter for this, but ideally in append mode this would need to detect if the global parameters are already there to not write them again.

cc @nden

                  'CRPIX2': 3.0453999e+03, 'CRVAL2': 4.388538000000e+01,
                  'PV2_1': 1., 'PV2_3': 220.})
-    # Just check that this doesn't raise an exception:
-    w.footprint_to_file(str(tmpdir.join('test.txt')))
+

+

title: Define __getslice__ and __setslice__ only on PY2 (if needed).
description:
Inspired by the removal of `__getslice__` and `__setslice__` from numpy (https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/8592/files), I looked through our code. These methods have been deprecated since 2.5 and in pure python will not get called at all in 2.7. However, for C code they do get called in python 2.7 , so anything depending on `ndarray` has to intercept them still. But only in python2, so I at least marked them with `if six.PY2`, so they will get automatically removed in astropy 3.0.

In the process, I also ensured that quantity item setting does not get slowed down if a quantity is not part of a table.

                      _wrapx, _unwrapx, _makep, Delayed)
 from .util import decode_ascii, encode_ascii
-from ...extern.six import string_types
+from ...extern.six import string_types, PY2
 from ...extern.six.moves import range, zip
 from ...utils import lazyproperty
 from ...utils.compat import suppress
@@ -96,9 +96,6 @@ class FITS_record(object):
 
         self.array.field(indx)[self.row] = value
 
-    def __getslice__(self, start, end):

             raise TypeError('Assignment requires a FITS_record, tuple, or '
                             'list as input.')
 
-    def __getslice__(self, start, end):
-        return self[slice(start, end)]
+    if PY2:

+            self.__setitem__(slice(start, end), value)

         """

title: Fix for pickling unregistered units
description:
My attempt at a fix that allows for pickling unregistered irreducible units. I have added comments for my (possibly flawed) understanding of the various stages of _recreate_irreducible_unit.

I also included a test case to check pickling works for unregistered units.

Reference:
#5867
diff:
diff --git a/astropy/units/core.py b/astropy/units/core.py
index 1568f3f7851..26f0dc9351c 100644
--- a/astropy/units/core.py
+++ b/astropy/units/core.py
@@ -1638,11 +1638,17 @@ def _recreate_irreducible_unit(cls, names, registered):
     """
     registry = get_current_unit_registry().registry
     if names[0] in registry:
+        # If in local registry return that object.
         return registry[names[0]]
     else:
         unit = cls(names)
         if registered:
+            # If not in local registry but registered in origin registry,
+            # enable unit in local registry.
             get_current_unit_registry().add_enabled_units([unit])
+        else:
+            # If not registered at all, just return the unit.
+            return unit
 
 
 class IrreducibleUnit(NamedUnit):
diff --git a/astropy/units/tests/test_units.py b/astropy/units/tests/test_units.py
index e63ac3821d6..cbb35a48c36 100644
--- a/astropy/units/tests/test_units.py
+++ b/astropy/units/tests/test_units.py
@@ -503,6 +503,13 @@ def test_pickling():
     assert other is u.m
 
     new_unit = u.IrreducibleUnit(['foo'], format={'baz': 'bar'})
+    # Test pickling unregistered unit
+    p = pickle.dumps(new_unit)
+    new_unit_copy = pickle.loads(p)
+    assert new_unit_copy.names == ['foo']
+    assert new_unit_copy.get_format_name('baz') == 'bar'
+
+    # Test pickling registered unit
     with u.add_enabled_units([new_unit]):
         p = pickle.dumps(new_unit)
         new_unit_copy = pickle.loads(p)

expected_findings.description: The reviewer (`mhvk`) pointed out that the introduced code failed to return the created `unit` when it was `registered` but not initially found in the local registry. The function would enable it but then implicitly return `None`. The reviewer suggested the fix (remove the `else` and always return the `unit` after potential registration), which was implemented in a subsequent commit by the reviewer themselves. A later comment by the reviewer confirmed this fix addressed an issue where loading pickled registered units would fail.

The reviewer (`mhvk`) observed that the newly added test case didn't sufficiently cover the behavior related to unit registration after unpickling (loading). Although mentioned as potentially outside the scope, the reviewer subsequently committed changes to enhance the test specifically to cover these registration aspects.

expected_findings.description: Reviewer `taldcroft` pointed out that using both `True` and `'force'` in the `parametrize` decorator for the `fast_reader` option was redundant, as `True` uses the fast reader if available, just like `'force'`. The reviewer suggested using only `'force'` (along with `False`) to make the test explicitly fail if the fast C reader wasn't available or failed, rather than potentially falling back to the Python reader silently. The author `dhomeier` acknowledged this ("Yes, that's what was happening in the first tests....").

Reviewer `taldcroft` pointed out that the assertions checking the resulting `dat.meta['comments']` and `dat.colnames` should be performed after *each* of the `ascii.read` calls within the test loop, not just some of them. This ensures the test correctly verifies the state after each manipulation and read operation. The author `dhomeier` initially asked for clarification but then acknowledged the oversight ("Oh, I see one `assert dat.meta['comments'] == comments` got lost...").

The ``LombScargle`` methods currently lack easy access to the maximum likelihood model parameters. This PR adds model inspection methods to the ``LombScargle`` class, adds a comprehensive set of unit tests for these, and adds a section to the lomb-scargle documentation outlining how to understand these methods.

+    def offset(self):
+        """Return the offset of the model
+        
+        The offset of the model is the (weighted) mean of the y values.
+        Note that if self.center_data is False, the offset is 0 by definition.
+
+        Returns
+        -------
+        offset : scalar
+
+        See Also
+        --------
+        design_matrix
+        model
+        model_parameters
+        """
+        y, dy = strip_units(self.y, self.dy)
+        if dy is None:
+            dy = 1
+        dy = np.broadcast_to(dy, y.shape)
+        if self.center_data:
+            w = dy ** -2.0
+            y_mean = np.dot(y, w) / w.sum()
+        else:
+            y_mean = 0
+        return y_mean * get_unit(self.y)
+
+    def model_parameters(self, frequency, units=True):
+        r"""Compute the best-fit model parameters at the given frequency.
+
+        The model described by these parameters is:
+
+        .. math::
+
+            y(t; f, \vec{\theta}) = \theta_0 + \sum_{n=1}^{\tt nterms} [\theta_{2n-1}\sin(2\pi n f t) + \theta_{2n}\cos(2\pi n f t)]
+ 
+        where :math:`\vec{\theta}` is the array of parameters returned by this function.
+
+        Parameters
+        ----------
+        t : array_like or Quantity, length n_samples
+            times at which to compute the model
+        frequency : float
+            the frequency for the model
+        units : bool
+            If True (default), return design matrix with data units.
+
+        Returns
+        -------
+        theta : np.ndarray (n_parameters,)
+            The best-fit model parameters at the given frequency.
+
+        See Also
+        --------
+        design_matrix
+        model
+        offset
+        """
+        frequency = self._validate_frequency(frequency)
+        t, y, dy = strip_units(self.t, self.y, self.dy)
+
+        if self.center_data:
+            y = y - strip_units(self.offset())
+
+        dy = np.ones_like(y) if dy is None else np.asarray(dy)
+        X = self.design_matrix(frequency)
+        parameters = np.linalg.solve(np.dot(X.T, X),
+                                     np.dot(X.T, y / dy))
+        if units:
+            parameters = get_unit(self.y) * parameters
+        return parameters
+
+    def design_matrix(self, frequency, t=None):
+        """Compute the design matrix for a given frequency
+
+        Parameters
+        ----------
+        frequency : float
+            the frequency for the model
+        t : array_like or Quantity, length n_samples
+            times at which to compute the model (optional). If not specified,

+            The design matrix for the model at the given frequency.
+
+        See Also
+        --------
+        model
+        model_parameters
+        offset
+        """
+        if t is None:
+            t, dy = strip_units(self.t, self.dy)
+        else:
+            t, dy = strip_units(self._validate_t(t), None)
+        return design_matrix(t, frequency, dy,
+                             nterms=self.nterms,
+                             bias=self.fit_mean)
+

title: Improve table Row and len() speed
description:
This makes table row access faster by about a factor of 2-3.  No API changes, just more efficient code. 

It also speeds up Table len() by a factor of 3-10.  This does remove doing a sanity check that all the columns have the same length, but there is no way a table should get into that state.  Also no obvious reason that the len() call should be the place to discover if a table has somehow become malformed.

 Below is the profiling code, with `t = simple_table(cols=25, size=100)`:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/348089/54120196-8168da80-43cd-11e9-92fb-6a1f6a14d633.png)

   converted to pandas by flattening the columns as necessary to plain

 import numpy as np
 
@@ -29,25 +30,32 @@ class Row:
     """
 
     def __init__(self, table, index):
-        self._table = table
-        self._index = operator.index(index)
+        # Get the length of the first column.  Rely on the table being well-formed
+        # at this point.
+        n = len(next(iter(table.columns.values())))
 
-        n = len(table)
         if index < -n or index >= n:
             raise IndexError('index {0} out of range for table with length {1}'
                              .format(index, len(table)))
 
-        # Ensure that the row index is positive [#8422]
-        self._index = self._index % n
-
-    def __getitem__(self, item):
-        if self._table._is_list_or_tuple_of_str(item):

-        else:

+                cols = [self._table[name] for name in item]
+                out = self._table.__class__(cols, copy=False)[self._index]
+            else:
+                # This is only to raise an exception
+                out = self._table.columns[item][self._index]
         return out

expected_findings.description: The reviewer (`mhvk`) questioned the optimization within `Row.__init__` (getting length from the first column) and suggested that the real performance bottleneck was likely `Table.__len__` itself, proposing to optimize that method instead. The author (`taldcroft`) agreed and implemented a significant optimization for `Table.__len__`, which also simplified the `Row.__init__` logic.

The reviewer (`mhvk`) suggested converting the input `index` to an integer using `operator_index` *before* performing the range check (`if index < -n or index >= n:`). This was proposed to provide clearer error messages if a non-integer type (like an array) was passed, as `operator_index` would raise a more specific `TypeError` earlier. The author (`taldcroft`) agreed and implemented the change.

After the logic in `Row.__init__` was changed (in commit `187aba7c`) to use `len(table)` again (following the optimization of `Table.__len__`), the comment explaining the previous approach (getting length from the first column) became obsolete. The reviewer (`mhvk`) pointed this out.

title: Use raise ... from to get tracebacks
description:
When an error occurs in format conversion, it is captured and re-raised
as a ValueError. This is necessary for format guessing but it can make
error reporting vague. Use raise ... from so that tracebacks go all the
way back to the line where the original exception was raised.

Specifically, the underlying data of the masked elements was ignored for column width calculation, leading to a smaller dtype (`U2`) than expected (`U3`) and potential data truncation if the mask was later removed. title: Make classproperty and lazyproperty thread-safe
description:
### Description
This pull request is to address thread safety in the decorator utilities.

Fixes #11221.

I've also added unit tests. Testing race conditions is notoriously tricky, so I've made it try 10000 times each. That adds about 1s (for each), which is my attempt at a compromise between not slowing down the tests and trying enough times to trigger the bug. Without the fix it is still not enough to reliably fail, but it should be enough that if someone breaks it in future it will fail sooner or later in CI and prompt someone to look closer.

 import inspect

+                                      sharedmethod, classproperty, lazyproperty,

     assert B.__dict__['foo'].__doc__ == "The foo."
 
 
+@pytest.fixture
+def fast_thread_switching():
+    """Fixture that reduces thread switching interval.
+
+    This makes it easier to provoke race conditions.
+    """
+    old = sys.getswitchinterval()
+    sys.setswitchinterval(1e-6)
+    yield
+    sys.setswitchinterval(old)
+
+
+def test_classproperty_lazy_threadsafe(fast_thread_switching):
+    """
+    Test that a class property with lazy=True is thread-safe.
+    """
+    workers = 8
+    with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=workers) as executor:
+        # This is testing for race conditions, so try many times in the
+        # hope that we'll get the timing right.
+        for p in range(10000):
+
+            class A:
+                @classproperty(lazy=True)
+                def foo(cls):
+                    nonlocal calls
+                    calls += 1
+                    return object()
+
+            # Have all worker threads query in parallel
+            calls = 0
+            futures = [executor.submit(lambda: A.foo) for i in range(workers)]
+            # Check that only one call happened and they all received it
+            values = [future.result() for future in futures]
+            assert calls == 1
+            assert values[0] is not None
+            assert values == [values[0]] * workers
+
+
+def test_lazyproperty_threadsafe(fast_thread_switching):
+    """
+    Test thread safety of lazyproperty.
+    """
+    # This test is generally similar to test_classproperty_lazy_threadsafe
+    # above. See there for comments.
+
+    class A:
+        def __init__(self):
+            self.calls = 0
+
+        @lazyproperty
+        def foo(self):
+            self.calls += 1
+            return object()
+
+    workers = 8
+    with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=workers) as executor:
+        for p in range(10000):
+            a = A()
+            futures = [executor.submit(lambda: a.foo) for i in range(workers)]
+            values = [future.result() for future in futures]
+            assert a.calls == 1
+            assert a.foo is not None
+            assert values == [a.foo] * workers
+
+
 def test_format_doc_stringInput_simple():
     # Simple tests with string input

expected_findings.description: Reviewer `pllim` questioned the placement of the `fast_thread_switching` fixture, suggesting it might be better defined using `setup_module`/`teardown_module` for the test module instead of being a local pytest fixture. The author (`bmerry`) disagreed with the `setup_module` approach due to potential performance impact on other tests but acknowledged the desire to avoid duplication, anticipating the fixture's use in other modules. This led to the decision to move the fixture to a shared location.

--- a/docs/modeling/physical_models.rst

@@ -288,3 +288,39 @@ The maximum circular velocity and radius of maximum circular velocity are availa
     # Display plot
     plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.03, 1, 0.95])
     plt.show()
+
+
+.. _Cosmologies:
+
+Cosmologies
+===========
+
+The instances of the |Cosmology| class (and subclasses) include
+|Cosmology.to_format|, a method to convert a Cosmology to another python
+object. Specifically, any redshift method can be converted to a
+:class:`~astropy.modeling.FittableModel` instance using the argument
+``format="astropy.model"``.
+During the conversion, each |Cosmology| :class:`~astropy.cosmology.Parameter`
+is converted to a :class:`astropy.modeling.Model`
+:class:`~astropy.modeling.Parameter`, while the redshift-method becomes the
+model's ``__call__`` / ``evaluate`` method.
+This means cosmologies can now be fit with data!
+
+.. code-block::
+
+    >>> from astropy.cosmology import Planck18
+    >>> model = Planck18.to_format(format="astropy.model", method="lookback_time")
+    >>> model
+    <FlatLambdaCDMCosmologyLookbackTimeModel(H0=67.66 km / (Mpc s), Om0=0.30966,
+        Tcmb0=2.7255 K, Neff=3.046, m_nu=[0.  , 0.  , 0.06] eV, Ob0=0.04897,
+        name='Planck18')>
+
+When finished, e.g. fitting, a model can be turned back into a |Cosmology|
+using |Cosmology.from_format|.
+
+.. code-block::
+
+    >>> from astropy.cosmology import Cosmology
+    >>> cosmo = Cosmology.from_format(model, format="astropy.model")
+    >>> cosmo == Planck18
+    True

expected_findings.description: Reviewer 'pllim' pointed out a documentation build error ("Undefined substitution referenced") caused by the newly added documentation lines using `|Cosmology.to_format|` and `|Cosmology.from_format|`. The developer ('nstarman', acting for the bot author) acknowledged the issue. Further discussion revealed that the definitions for these substitutions were missing in this backport branch because a related commit from another PR (#12611) hadn't been included.

This pull request is to address a feature request in https://community.openastronomy.org/t/converting-astropy-time-time-to-datetime-leapseconds/637 for a way to convert times within a leap second to `datetime` format.

Apply "skip-basebranch-check" label **before** you open the PR! -->

This pull request is to address a problem I encountered when reading Table 4 of [Kirkpatrick et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJS..271...55K/abstract) ([link to table in .txt format](https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/0067-0049/271/2/55/revision2/apjsad24e2t4_mrt.txt)). Only the last 18 rows of the table were read. I realized this was because the [`CdsData`](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/177da898ddc7686a5a757225e73011e94db31b10/astropy/io/ascii/cds.py?plain=1#L205) class defines section delimiters as lines starting with 6 dashes (`-`) or equal signs (`=`). The table mentioned above uses dashes at the start of line to indicate indentation and has lines with 6 or more dashes before a regular row.

I added a minimal version of the table to the test cases for `test_read.py`. I also added a simple fix that keeps the existing `x.startswith("------")` check but adds `len(set(x)) == 1` to ensure that the line only contains dashes. I implemented this fix in a private function as there where 3 instances of this check.

This fix assumes that section delimiter lines will always only contain equals or dashes. **I am not sure this assumption is correct** (but I think so, based on what documentation I could find for CDS and MRT formats). If it is not, we would need to check that what comes after the dashes or equals is not a regular row (I'm not sure how to do that but the existing column and splitter definitions would probably help).

This is my first PR, so let me know if there are things I should add or do differently!

Thank you!
diff:
diff --git a/astropy/io/ascii/cds.py b/astropy/io/ascii/cds.py
index 176d5823439..815bec8b8df 100644
--- a/astropy/io/ascii/cds.py
+++ b/astropy/io/ascii/cds.py
@@ -21,6 +21,27 @@ from . import core, fixedwidth
 __doctest_skip__ = ["*"]
 
 
+def _is_section_delimiter(line):
+    """Check if line is a section delimiter
+
+    CDS/MRT tables use dashes or equal signs ("------" or "======") to
+    separate sections. This function checks if a line contains only either
+    of these characters.
+
+    Parameters
+    ----------
+    line : str
+        String containing an entire line from the table text file.
+
+    Returns
+    -------
+    bool
+        True if the line is a section delimiter, False otherwise.
+
+    """
+    return line.startswith(("------", "=======")) and len(set(line)) == 1
+
+
 class CdsHeader(core.BaseHeader):
     _subfmt = "CDS"
 
@@ -67,7 +88,7 @@ class CdsHeader(core.BaseHeader):
                 line = line.strip()
                 if in_header:
                     lines.append(line)
-                    if line.startswith(("------", "=======")):
+                    if _is_section_delimiter(line):
                         comment_lines += 1
                         if comment_lines == 3:
                             break
@@ -117,7 +138,7 @@ class CdsHeader(core.BaseHeader):
 
         cols = []
         for line in itertools.islice(lines, i_col_def + 4, None):
-            if line.startswith(("------", "=======")):
+            if _is_section_delimiter(line):
                 break
             match = re_col_def.match(line)
             if match:
@@ -216,9 +237,10 @@ class CdsData(core.BaseData):
         # attribute.
         if self.header.readme and self.table_name:
             return lines
-        i_sections = [
-            i for i, x in enumerate(lines) if x.startswith(("------", "======="))
-        ]
+        # Check that line starts with either 6 "-" or "="
+        # and that it contains only a single repeated character.
+        # Latter condition fixes cases where a regular row starts with 6 "-"
+        i_sections = [i for i, x in enumerate(lines) if _is_section_delimiter(x)]
         if not i_sections:
             raise core.InconsistentTableError(
                 f"No {self._subfmt} section delimiter found"

title: Optimize getting config item values
description:
Fix #12504 (I think, doing better might be possible but not sure without breaking some feature of our complicated configuration system):

As explained there, getting a config item is quite slow, values being stored within the ConfigObj object . And io.fits accesses config items when e.g. accessing the value of a card, this means a lot of config item calls for tables especially with many columns. 

So here I'm adding a cache on the ConfigItem descriptor, allowing to get the key much faster while still storing its value on the ConfigObj object.

expected_findings.description: The reviewer (`charettes`) pointed out that the `import re` statement was placed locally inside a method and suggested moving it to the global scope (top level of the file), which is standard Python practice for clarity and organization. The developer acknowledged this by implementing the change in a subsequent commit.

The reviewer (`timgraham`) evaluated the overall approach introduced in the PR (saving change messages in English and parsing them later using regex for translation/display) and deemed it "too brittle". URLs with un-escaped "/", "@" or ":" characters in the username or password fields should be rejected. This fix replaces the `\S` set with its equivalent `[^\s]`, and then adds the above characters to the exclusion set, giving `[^\s:@/]`.

title: Fixed #32443 -- Removed "shifted" CSS class when admin's sidebar is disabled.
description:
Hi

I faced an issue in disabling the nav-sidebar. When I disable the nav-sidebar using `admin.site.enable_nav_sidebar = False`, the `shifted` class is still remaining, because this class is hard-coded in the `main` tag. I remove the hard-coded class and add the `shifted` class whenever we have the `side-navbar` element on the page.

expected_findings.description: The reviewer (felixxm) pointed out that the added check `navSidebar &&` in the `main.classList.toggle` call was unnecessary because the script `nav_sidebar.js` itself is only loaded when the sidebar is enabled, implying `navSidebar` would exist. The developer acknowledged this implicitly by removing the check in a subsequent commit, referencing this reason in the commit message.

The reviewer (felixxm) suggested adding a test assertion to verify that the `main` div does not have the `shifted` class when the sidebar is disabled, complementing the code change made in the PR. The developer implemented this suggestion in the next commit, adding a similar assertion (though in a different test method).

title: BUG: Fix streamplot when velocity component is exactly zero.
description:
When one component of the velocity field is zero, streamplot fails to draw streamlines. Here's a short example of the issue:

``` python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

N = 10
Y, X = np.mgrid[:N, :N]
U = np.ones((N, N))
V = np.zeros((N, N))

plt.streamplot(X, Y, U, V)
plt.show()
```

Explanation of fix:
Negative and positive steps are treated differently by the code. Before, a zero gradient (`cx`, `cy`) was getting treated as a negative step. This resulted in a step size of `-inf`; treating zero as a positive step results in a step size of (positive) `inf`. This `inf` value gets filtered out since the integration routine chooses the smaller of the two (`dsx`, `dsy`) step sizes.
diff:
diff --git a/lib/matplotlib/streamplot.py b/lib/matplotlib/streamplot.py
index a3a349a74fe..8022f7d3fc9 100644
--- a/lib/matplotlib/streamplot.py
+++ b/lib/matplotlib/streamplot.py
@@ -461,14 +461,14 @@ def _euler_step(xf_traj, yf_traj, dmap, f):
     xi = xf_traj[-1]
     yi = yf_traj[-1]
     cx, cy = f(xi, yi)
-    if cx > 0:
-        dsx = (nx - 1 - xi) / cx
-    else:
+    if cx < 0:
         dsx = xi / -cx
-    if cy > 0:
-        dsy = (ny - 1 - yi) / cy
     else:
+        dsx = (nx - 1 - xi) / cx
+    if cy < 0:
         dsy = yi / -cy
+    else:
+        dsy = (ny - 1 - yi) / cy
     ds = min(dsx, dsy)
     xf_traj.append(xi + cx*ds)
     yf_traj.append(yi + cy*ds)

expected_findings.description: Reviewer `efiring` explicitly stated that the approach introduced in the first commit (implicitly handling zero velocity components `cx` or `cy` via division, potentially resulting in division by zero and relying on `inf`) was problematic, could raise warnings, or even fail. The author (`tonysyu`) acknowledged this ("Yeah, it felt a little flakey to me too") and proposed explicitly checking for zero and setting the step size to `inf`. The reviewer (`efiring`) agreed with this proposed solution.

title: Building Matplotlib on Ubuntu
description:
Hi,
I experienced a problem when compiling matplotlib on Ubuntu 13.04. The setup determined that the freetype2 headers are not installed (although they are). The reason for this is a function in setupext.py script that searches for "ft2build.h" in the freetype2 include directories ("/usr/include/freetype2" and below), whereas the file resides in "/usr/include/ft2build.h". As a quick workaround, I linked /usr/include/ft2build.h to /usr/include/freetype2/ft2build.h and matplotlib compiled just fine.

I don't know it this has been caused by a change in the ubuntu package or by a modification in setupext.py though..

title: Look for user-specified styles in ~/.config/matplotlib/stylelib
description:
Hi all,
I just noticed that the `styles` module currently only looks for user-specified styles in  `~/.matplotlib/stylelib`. I think it ought to also look in `~/.config/matplotlib/stylelib/` for consistency with `~/.config/matplotlib/matplotlibrc` and in order to comply with the [latest XDG standard](http://standards.freedesktop.org/basedir-spec/basedir-spec-latest.html) (c.f. #454).

 _here = os.path.abspath(os.path.dirname(__file__))

 # Users may want multiple library paths, so store a list of paths.
-USER_LIBRARY_PATHS = [os.path.join('~', '.matplotlib', 'stylelib')]
+USER_LIBRARY_PATHS = [os.path.join('~', '.matplotlib', 'stylelib'), 
+                      os.path.join('~', '.config', 'matplotlib', 'stylelib')]
 STYLE_EXTENSION = 'mplstyle'
 STYLE_FILE_PATTERN = re.compile('([\S]+).%s$' % STYLE_EXTENSION)

Reviewer `pelson` suggested using the internal function `matplotlib._get_configdir()` instead of manually constructing the path using `os.path.join('~', '.config', ...)` and `os.path.join('~', '.matplotlib', ...)`. This promotes consistency with how other configuration paths are handled in matplotlib and is a more robust solution approach. The author accepted this suggestion and implemented it. title: Python 3 METH_VARARGS with METH_KEYWORDS
description:
Added `METH_VARARGS` to the method definition flags in __macosx.m_ as Python 3 requires `METH_VARARGS` to be set when `METH_KEYWORDS` is set. This is already the case where `METH_KEYWORDS` is used elsewhere, namely __ttconv.cpp_ and _cntr.c_.

Without this and executing within Python3 one will get the error
`SystemError: Bad call flags in PyCFunction_Call. METH_OLDARGS is no longer supported!`

diff --git a/src/_macosx.m b/src/_macosx.m
index aaa125806f6..1a60bb70d56 100644
--- a/src/_macosx.m
+++ b/src/_macosx.m
@@ -3779,12 +3779,12 @@ static PyMethodDef FigureCanvas_methods[] = {
     },
     {"start_event_loop",
      (PyCFunction)FigureCanvas_start_event_loop,
-     METH_KEYWORDS,
+     METH_KEYWORDS | METH_VARARGS,
      "Runs the event loop until the timeout or until stop_event_loop is called.\n",
     },
     {"stop_event_loop",
      (PyCFunction)FigureCanvas_stop_event_loop,
-     METH_KEYWORDS,
+     METH_KEYWORDS | METH_VARARGS,
      "Stops the event loop that was started by start_event_loop.\n",
     },
     {NULL}  /* Sentinel */

expected_findings.description: The reviewer (`mdehoon`) noted that while the change was correct for `start_event_loop`, the `stop_event_loop` function takes no arguments and therefore should use the `METH_NOARGS` flag instead of `METH_KEYWORDS | METH_VARARGS` which was introduced in the initial commit. The author (`cimarronm`) acknowledged this was correct and pushed a fix.

title: Issue with iterability of axes arguments [backport to 1.4.x]
description:
I have been trying to use the `_as_mpl_axes` method to create a custom projection. I am returning an Axes subclass and a dictionary of arguments to pass to the class. One of the arguments is an item of type `astropy.wcs.WCS`. In `figure.py`, the following code:

```
        def fixitems(items):
            #items may have arrays and lists in them, so convert them
            # to tuples for the key
            ret = []
            for k, v in items:
                if iterable(v):
                    v = tuple(v)
                ret.append((k, v))
            return tuple(ret)
```

results in an error, specifically when doing `tuple(v)`. The issue is that `iterable(wcs)` returns `True` but `tuple(wcs)` crashes. As a general issue, `iter(v)` working does not guarantee that `tuple(v)` will work. One solution is to simply do:

```
if iterable(v):
    try:
        v = tuple(v)
    except:
        pass
```

I'm not sure if there is a better way to deal with this kind of issue. Just for the record, `tuple(wcs)` gives:

```
ValueError: Cannot downsample a WCS with indexing.  Use wcs.sub or wcs.dropaxis if you want to remove axes.
```

To some extent, the issue here is that while `WCS` has a `__getitem__` method, it is not strictly iterable. So maybe the issue is actually that `iterable` should not rely just on `iter`. Maybe the `iterable` function:

```

def iterable(obj):
    'return true if *obj* is iterable'
    try:
        iter(obj)
    except TypeError:
        return False
    return True
```

in `cbook.py` should be using:

```
next(iter(wcs))
```

? (which does raise an error in my case)

cc @mdboom, since it involves the WCS class.

diff --git a/lib/matplotlib/figure.py b/lib/matplotlib/figure.py

@@ -786,7 +786,13 @@ class Figure(Artist):
             ret = []
             for k, v in items:
                 if iterable(v):
-                    v = tuple(v)
+                    # some objects can define __getitem__ without being 
+                    # iterable and in those cases the conversion to tuples 
+                    # will fail.
+                    try:
+                        v = tuple(v)
+                    except:
+                        pass
                 ret.append((k, v))
             return tuple(ret)

title: Make sure that initial state gets reset if anything goes wrong in ``rc_context`` [backport to 1.4.x]
description:
Fixed a bug that caused rc parameters to not be reset to initial state if an exception happened while setting new rc parameters inside rc_context. This matters because I use `rc_context` is a testing suite and one of my tests may _want_ `rc_context` to fail, but then the rcparams are left in a modified state for future tests. I have included a regression test.

Unfortunately I have to use an ordered dict otherwise the failure is not deterministic (because it depends on the order in which the rcparams are set) so if ordered dict can't import I simply pass the test (I wasn't sure if you make use of the skipping plugin).
diff:
diff --git a/lib/matplotlib/__init__.py b/lib/matplotlib/__init__.py
index e07a6fd13e8..a7034c47f95 100644
--- a/lib/matplotlib/__init__.py
+++ b/lib/matplotlib/__init__.py
@@ -1249,10 +1249,15 @@ class rc_context(object):
         self.rcdict = rc
         self.fname = fname
         self._rcparams = rcParams.copy()
-        if self.fname:
-            rc_file(self.fname)
-        if self.rcdict:
-            rcParams.update(self.rcdict)
+        try:
+            if self.fname:
+                rc_file(self.fname)
+            if self.rcdict:
+                rcParams.update(self.rcdict)
+        except:
+            # if anything goes wrong, revert rc parameters and re-raise
+            rcParams.update(self._rcparams)
+            raise
 
     def __enter__(self):
         return self

     key_list = [k for k in mpl.rcParams if 'keymap' in k]
     for k in key_list:
         assert(isinstance(mpl.rcParams[k], list))
+
+
+def test_rcparams_reset_after_fail():
+
+    # There was previously a bug that meant that if rc_context failed and
+    # raised an exception due to issues in the supplied rc parameters, the
+    # global rc parameters were left in a modified state.
+
+    try:
+        from collections import OrderedDict
+    except:
+        return  # can't run this test on Python 2.6
+
+    with mpl.rc_context(rc={'text.usetex': False}):
+
+        assert mpl.rcParams['text.usetex'] is False
+
+        with assert_raises(KeyError):
+            with mpl.rc_context(rc=OrderedDict([('text.usetex', True),('test.blah', True)])):
+                pass
+
+        assert mpl.rcParams['text.usetex'] is False

expected_findings.description: The reviewer (`WeatherGod`) questioned whether simply updating `rcParams` with the old values (`_rcparams`) would correctly reset the state if new keys were added before the exception occurred (e.g., `test.blah` in the test case). The author (`astrofrog`) acknowledged this ("ah yes, good catch") and implemented a fix.

The reviewer (`WeatherGod`) pointed out that a bare `except:` should be avoided and suggested catching the specific `ImportError` expected. The author (`astrofrog`) acknowledged this and fixed it in the next commit.

The reviewer (`tacaswell`) suggested that instead of silently returning (which skips the test without clear reporting), the standard `SkipTest` exception from the `nose` framework should be raised. They also suggested checking the Python version directly (`sys.version_info`) rather than relying on the `ImportError`. The author (`astrofrog`) agreed ("I'm fine with picky :)") and implemented the suggested approach.

title: Update to score_family in font_manager.py
description:
This PR fixes the score calculation for the case of matching a generic font name given in the `families` list.

The returned score is now constrained by the position `i` of the match in the list. If the font being scored (`family2`) is the first choice for that generic name in rcParams, it will receive the same score as if it were an exact match for that position in the `families` list, namely `i / len(families)`. If the font being scored is in the alias list but not the first choice, the returned score will be greater than `i / len(families)` but less than `(i + 1) / len(families)`, ensuring that the preferred order of fonts listed in both `families` and rcParams font alias list are respected.
diff:
diff --git a/lib/matplotlib/font_manager.py b/lib/matplotlib/font_manager.py
index 91fe97e128f..a94e98ef594 100644
--- a/lib/matplotlib/font_manager.py
+++ b/lib/matplotlib/font_manager.py
@@ -1099,15 +1099,16 @@ class FontManager(object):
         Returns a match score between the list of font families in
         *families* and the font family name *family2*.
 
-        An exact match anywhere in the list returns 0.0.
+        An exact match at the head of the list returns 0.0.
 
-        A match by generic font name will return 0.1.
+        A match further down the list will return between 0 and 1.
 
         No match will return 1.0.
         """
         if not isinstance(families, (list, tuple)):
             families = [families]
         family2 = family2.lower()
+        step = 1 / len(families)
         for i, family1 in enumerate(families):
             family1 = family1.lower()
             if family1 in font_family_aliases:
@@ -1117,12 +1118,11 @@ class FontManager(object):
                 options = [x.lower() for x in options]
                 if family2 in options:
                     idx = options.index(family2)
-                    return ((0.1 * (idx / len(options))) *
-                            ((i + 1) / len(families)))
+                    return (i + idx / len(options)) * step
             elif family1 == family2:
                 # The score should be weighted by where in the
                 # list the font was found.
-                return i / len(families)
+                return i * step
         return 1.0
 
     def score_style(self, style1, style2):

expected_findings.description: The reviewer `tacaswell` suggested adding parentheses to the calculation `(i + idx / len(options)) * step` to make the order of operations explicit for better readability. The author implemented this suggestion in the next commit without further discussion, implicitly confirming the change.

The reviewer `mdboom` pointed out that the calculation `step = 1 / len(families)` introduced in the first commit would cause a `ZeroDivisionError` if the input `families` list was empty. They suggested adding a check for this edge case. The author `chadawagner` acknowledged this ("Agreed, although it never checked before. Not a bad idea tho to be safe.", "Thanks for catching that!") and implemented the suggested check.

The idea of this is to be able set the seed points for the streamlines manually. I needed this because I was using it for magnetic field visualisation, which is more physical if you have a few long lines rather than lots of short ones, and I also wanted to seed them at the point in the domain which lead to the best integration.

expected_findings.description: Reviewer `tacaswell` pointed out that the new keyword argument `start_points` was added before existing keyword arguments (`transform`, `zorder`) in the function signatures for `streamplot` across multiple files. This breaks backward compatibility if users were previously relying on the positional order of those arguments. The developer implicitly acknowledged this by fixing the order in the subsequent commit.

Reviewer `efiring` questioned the clarity and correctness of the docstring for the new `start_points` parameter, specifically the phrase "In array coordinates." The developer (`Cadair`) confirmed this was an oversight and agreed that it should refer to data coordinates.

title: Two bugs in colors.BoundaryNorm
description:
**Bug 1: calling BoundaryNorm with a scalar**

Short discussion on the ML: http://matplotlib.1069221.n5.nabble.com/Misleading-BoundaryNorm-error-td45970.html
I added some extra tests to the previous test-suite which was quite short.

**Bug 2: clipping was ignored**

The previous call to np.clip was silently useless (not in place). I don't think that clipping makes much sense in the case of BoundaryNorm but still.
Before merging, I'd like to discuss the point I mention in the code comments: what about clipping the max values? Currently this is inconsistent and I'd like to change it, but I'd like to have your opinion on it. 

_disclaimer: this is my first PR, I hope to have done everything right. I did not see the "maintenance" branch so I branched from master. I think there are a couple of thing we can do better with these normalizing tools but I need more time to think about it..._

expected_findings.description: The reviewer (WeatherGod) pointed out that checking `not mask` would fail for array masks (non-trivial masked arrays), only working for scalar `False` masks. The author (fmaussion) acknowledged this ("Correct, masked arrays have not been tested yet...") and subsequent discussion (with efiring) covered how best to handle masked arrays and NaNs, leading to the use of `masked_invalid` and eventually `self.process_value`.

The reviewer (WeatherGod) questioned the accuracy of the comment `# ISSUE here: clip is ignored`, implying the `np.clip` call should handle it. The author (fmaussion) clarified that while `np.clip` worked on `xx`, the subsequent line `iret[xx >= self.vmax] = self.Ncmap` unconditionally assigned the "over" value (`self.Ncmap`) to any value equal to or greater than `self.vmax`. This meant that even when `clip=True`, values equal to `self.vmax` were mapped to `self.Ncmap` instead of the highest valid color index (`self.Ncmap - 1`), making the clipping ineffective for the upper bound.

title: TST: properly fence-post qt{4,5} backend tests
description:
This issue is that the new 'default' qt version is 5 if it is
available.  In the tests the backend is Agg so we are hitting the
fall through behavior.  If both pyqt4 and pyqt5 are installed, then
`QtCore` will be from PyQt5, but the backend_qt4Agg code assumes that it
is seeing the PyQt4 version of the classes.  This results in error on
`__init__` due to the change between PyQt4 and PyQt5.

Added test_backend_qt5.py to white listed tests.

closes #5194

title: FIX: subtle race condition in cbook.mkdirs
description: attn @timj
diff:
diff --git a/lib/matplotlib/cbook.py b/lib/matplotlib/cbook.py
index bc7e4df568b..d5f2ffbf776 100644
--- a/lib/matplotlib/cbook.py
+++ b/lib/matplotlib/cbook.py
@@ -1012,18 +1012,26 @@ def mkdirs(newdir, mode=0o777):
         > mkdir -p NEWDIR
         > chmod MODE NEWDIR
     """
-    try:
-        if not os.path.exists(newdir):
-            parts = os.path.split(newdir)
-            for i in range(1, len(parts) + 1):
-                thispart = os.path.join(*parts[:i])
-                if not os.path.exists(thispart):
-                    os.makedirs(thispart, mode)
-
-    except OSError as err:
-        # Reraise the error unless it's about an already existing directory
-        if err.errno != errno.EEXIST or not os.path.isdir(newdir):
-            raise
+    # this functionality is now in core python as of 3.2
+    if six.PY3:
+        os.makedirs(newdir, mode=mode, exist_ok=True)
+        return
+
+
+    def _make_leaf(newdir, mode):
+        if os.path.exists(newdir):
+            return
+        try:
+            os.makedirs(thispart, mode)
+        except OSError as err:
+            # Reraise the error unless it's about an already existing directory
+            if err.errno != errno.EEXIST or not os.path.isdir(newdir):
+                raise
+
+    parts = os.path.split(newdir)
+    for i in range(1, len(parts) + 1):
+        thispart = os.path.join(*parts[:i])
+        _make_leaf(thispart, mode)
 
 
 class GetRealpathAndStat(object):

expected_findings.description: Reviewer `timj` questioned the necessity of using `os.makedirs` within the loop structure designed for Python 2, suggesting `os.mkdir` might be more appropriate given the loop was handling parent directories. The author (`tacaswell`) acknowledged this ("Good point, simplified.") and proceeded to simplify the entire Python 2 codepath.

Reviewer `mdboom` suggested restructuring the code to use an `if/else` block instead of `if/return` followed by the Python 2 code. This was proposed for improved clarity and to make future removal of the Python 2 code easier. The author (`tacaswell`) agreed ("done. That make lots of sense...") and implemented the change.

title: Fix to csv2rec bug for review
description:
Datetime strings in csv files in dayfirst or yearfirst format with
nonzero hour&minute&second will not be properly represented. Date
strings will, presuming the csv file contains no strings in that column
that have nonzero hour/minute/second components in a datetime string. Refer to issue #6184 for further information.

@@ -2833,7 +2833,13 @@ def csv2rec(fname, comments='#', skiprows=0, checkrows=0, delimiter=',',
             raise ValueError('invalid bool')
 
     dateparser = dateutil.parser.parse
-    mydateparser = with_default_value(dateparser, datetime.date(1, 1, 1))
+
+    def mydateparser(x):
+        # try and return a datetime object
+        d = dateparser(x, dayfirst=dayfirst, yearfirst=yearfirst)
+        return d
+    mydateparser = with_default_value(mydateparser, datetime.datetime(1,1,1,0,0,0))
+
     myfloat = with_default_value(float, np.nan)
     myint = with_default_value(int, -1)
     mystr = with_default_value(str, '')

title: shims for categorical support for numpy < 1.8
description:
Matplotlib doesn't render unicode strings with numpy below 1.7 and numpy below 1.8 is buggy with mixed type arrays, truncating strings to the size of the smallest string in the mixed type array. This PR introduces a shim that converts mixed type elements to strings before converting the input into an array, and it has a shim that decodes and encodes unicode, essentially forcing it into utf endpoint ASCII gibberish. 

This PR closes #7988

## PR Checklist

- [x] Has Pytest style unit tests
- [x] Code is PEP 8 compliant

+# np 1.6/1.7 support
+from distutils.version import LooseVersion
+import collections
+
+
+def shim_array(data):
+    if LooseVersion(np.__version__) <= LooseVersion('1.8.0'):
+        if (isinstance(data, six.string_types) or
+                not isinstance(data, collections.Iterable)):
+            data = [data]
+        try:
+            data = [str(d) for d in data]
+        except UnicodeEncodeError:
+            # this yields gibberish but unicode text doesn't
+            # render under numpy1.6 anyway
+            data = [d.encode('utf-8', 'ignore').decode('utf-8')
+                    for d in data]
+
+    return np.array(data, dtype=np.unicode)
+

title: use validate_[cap/join]style
description:
## PR Summary

Something trivial I found while scrolling around making sure I covered every join/capstyle we allow. Currently, `collections.py`, `rcparams.py`, and `lines.py` all have their own way of checking whether a cap/join-style is valid (`patches.py` uses the code from `lines.py`). These all boil down to a `cbook._check_in_list`, but some forget to warn that case-insensitivity is deprecated.

Since `rcparams.py` seems like the centralized place for checking that parameters are valid, I had them all call `rcparams.validate_[cap|join]style()` instead. This correctly warns for deprecated case-insensitivity.

title: BUG: Convert from str to writer on 3.2.x
description:
Just taking a simple [animation example](https://matplotlib.org/gallery/animation/animate_decay.html) and trying to use `anim.save(..., writer='imagemagick')` when it's not available on the platform produces on v3.2.x (it's fine on `master` but is [breaking some CIs currently](https://ci.appveyor.com/project/sphinx-gallery/sphinx-gallery/builds/33742826/job/5849j56nuga46609) that use 3.2):
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "ani.py", line 45, in <module>
    ani.save('temp.gif', writer='imagemagick')
  File "/home/larsoner/python/matplotlib/lib/matplotlib/animation.py", line 1109, in save
    writer = alt_writer(
TypeError: 'str' object is not callable
```
On this PR:
```
MovieWriter imagemagick unavailable; trying to use pillow instead.
```
Code I used to test:

<details>

```
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.animation as animation
from matplotlib.animation import ImageMagickWriter


def data_gen():
    for cnt in range(10):
        t = cnt / 10
        yield t, np.sin(2*np.pi*t) * np.exp(-t/10.)


def init():
    ax.set_ylim(-1.1, 1.1)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 10)
    del xdata[:]
    del ydata[:]
    line.set_data(xdata, ydata)
    return line,

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
line, = ax.plot([], [], lw=2)
ax.grid()
xdata, ydata = [], []


def run(data):
    # update the data
    t, y = data
    xdata.append(t)
    ydata.append(y)
    xmin, xmax = ax.get_xlim()

    if t >= xmax:
        ax.set_xlim(xmin, 2*xmax)
        ax.figure.canvas.draw()
    line.set_data(xdata, ydata)

    return line,


ImageMagickWriter.isAvailable = lambda: False  # emulate not available on the platform
ani = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, run, data_gen, blit=False, interval=10,
                              repeat=False, init_func=init)
ani.save('temp.gif', writer='imagemagick')
```

</details>

…tly have kward to set label fonts

## PR Summary
Based on new feature request from, https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/issues/18425
In order to complete these, I added another kwarg keyword, 'labelfont' in the Line2D object in matplotlib/lines.py and added relevant getter/setter functions. A keyword was also added in axis.py where parameters are actually applied.

This will allow a user to call tick_params and set the font family separate from the rest of the text on the figure without having to also invoke set_ylabels using axes.
